claim: PrPC is highly expressed in the nervous system.
source: The prion protein (PrPC) is highly expressed in the nervous system and critically involved in prion diseases where it misfolds into pathogenic PrPSc.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a known characteristic of PrPC.

claim: PrPC is critically involved in prion diseases where it misfolds into pathogenic PrPSc.
source: The prion protein (PrPC) is highly expressed in the nervous system and critically involved in prion diseases where it misfolds into pathogenic PrPSc.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in prion biology, stated in the abstract.

claim: PrPC has been suggested as a receptor mediating neurotoxicity in Alzheimer's disease.
source: Moreover, it has been suggested as a receptor mediating neurotoxicity in common neurodegenerative proteinopathies such as Alzheimer's disease.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature as indicated in the introduction section.

claim: PrPC is shed at the plasma membrane by the metalloprotease ADAM10.
source: PrPC is shed at the plasma membrane by the metalloprotease ADAM10, yet the impact of this on prion disease remains enigmatic.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by the authors' previous work and other citations.

claim: Depletion of ADAM10 in forebrain neurons leads to posttranslational increase of PrPC levels.
source: Employing conditional knockout mice, we show that depletion of ADAM10 in forebrain neurons leads to posttranslational increase of PrPC levels.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Lack of ADAM10 significantly reduces incubation times in prion-infected mice.
source: Upon prion infection of these mice, clinical, biochemical, and morphological data reveal that lack of ADAM10 significantly reduces incubation times and increases PrPSc formation.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by survival data in Figure 4 and Table 1.

claim: Lack of ADAM10 increases PrPSc formation.
source: Upon prion infection of these mice, clinical, biochemical, and morphological data reveal that lack of ADAM10 significantly reduces incubation times and increases PrPSc formation.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by Western blot and immunohistochemical data in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: Absence of shedding impairs spread of prion pathology.
source: In contrast, spatiotemporal analysis indicates that absence of shedding impairs spread of prion pathology.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunohistochemical analysis in Figure 8.

claim: ADAM10-mediated shedding has a dual role in prion disease.
source: Our data support a dual role for ADAM10-mediated shedding and highlight the role of proteolytic processing in prion disease.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, inferred from multiple experimental findings.

claim: PrPC is a glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI)-anchored lipid raft constituent.
source: The cellular prion protein (PrPC) is a glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI)-anchored lipid raft constituent highly expressed in neurons of the central nervous system (CNS).
evidence: This is established knowledge about PrPC structure and localization.

claim: Misfolding of PrPC into PrPSc occurs by a self-perpetuating process of templated conformational conversion.
source: Misfolding of PrPC into its pathogenic isoform, PrPSc, occurs by a self-perpetuating process of templated conformational conversion and causes transmissible and invariably fatal prion diseases (Prusiner, 1982).
evidence: This is a fundamental concept in prion biology, supported by citation to Prusiner, 1982.

claim: PrPC is a prerequisite of prion-associated neurotoxicity.
source: In these diseases, PrPC not only represents the substrate for conversion but also a prerequisite of prion-associated neurotoxicity (Büeler et al., 1993; Brandner et al., 1996; Mallucci et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior experimental work.

claim: PrPSc is prone to aggregation.
source: In contrast to PrPC, PrPSc is prone to aggregation and is characterized by a high β-sheet content and partial resistance to digestion with proteinase K (PK).
evidence: This is established knowledge about PrPSc properties.

claim: PrPSc is characterized by a high β-sheet content.
source: In contrast to PrPC, PrPSc is prone to aggregation and is characterized by a high β-sheet content and partial resistance to digestion with proteinase K (PK).
evidence: This is established knowledge about PrPSc structure.

claim: PrPSc is partially resistant to digestion with proteinase K.
source: In contrast to PrPC, PrPSc is prone to aggregation and is characterized by a high β-sheet content and partial resistance to digestion with proteinase K (PK).
evidence: This is a standard biochemical property used to detect PrPSc.

claim: PrPSc constitutes an essential component of infectious prion particles.
source: Moreover, PrPSc constitutes an essential component of infectious prion particles or 'prions' (Prusiner, 1982; Silveira et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to foundational prion research.

claim: PrPC acts as a neuronal receptor for neurotoxic amyloid-β oligomers.
source: Recently, a central role in more common proteinopathies, such as Alzheimer's disease (AD), has been attributed to PrPC where it was shown to act as a neuronal receptor for neurotoxic amyloid-β (Aβ) oligomers (Lauren et al., 2009; Dohler et al., 2014) and a variety of other disease-associated β-sheet rich protein assemblies including PrPSc (Resenberger et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior studies.

claim: PrPC binds to a variety of disease-associated β-sheet rich protein assemblies including PrPSc.
source: Recently, a central role in more common proteinopathies, such as Alzheimer's disease (AD), has been attributed to PrPC where it was shown to act as a neuronal receptor for neurotoxic amyloid-β (Aβ) oligomers (Lauren et al., 2009; Dohler et al., 2014) and a variety of other disease-associated β-sheet rich protein assemblies including PrPSc (Resenberger et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Resenberger et al., 2011.

claim: Binding of pathogenic oligomers to the flexible N-terminus of PrPC initiates a cascade of events that mediates neurotoxicity.
source: Despite some degree of controversy regarding this receptor function and its relevance in AD (Balducci et al., 2010; Benilova and De Strooper, 2010; Calella et al., 2010; Kessels et al., 2010), binding of pathogenic oligomers to the flexible N-terminus of PrPC is thought to initiate a cascade of events that mediates their neurotoxicity and results in synaptic degeneration and neuronal loss (Resenberger et al., 2011; Larson et al., 2012; Um et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations and represents a proposed mechanism.

claim: PrPC is subject to two conserved proteolytic cleavage events under physiological conditions, termed α-cleavage and shedding.
source: PrPC is subject to two conserved proteolytic cleavage events under physiological conditions, termed α-cleavage and shedding (Borchelt et al., 1993; Harris et al., 1993; Chen et al., 1995; Mange et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: α-cleavage occurs in the middle of the PrPC sequence and produces a soluble N1 and a membrane-attached C1 fragment.
source: While α-cleavage, occurring in the middle of the PrPC sequence and producing a soluble N1 and a membrane-attached C1 fragment, confers neuroprotection with regard to prion diseases (Lewis et al., 2009; Westergard et al., 2011; Turnbaugh et al., 2012; Campbell et al., 2013) and Aβ-associated neurotoxicity (Guillot-Sestier et al., 2009; Resenberger et al., 2011; Beland et al., 2012; Guillot-Sestier et al., 2012; Fluharty et al., 2013), the role of an extreme C-terminal cleavage in close proximity to the plasma membrane, termed shedding, remains enigmatic.
evidence: This is established knowledge about α-cleavage.

claim: α-cleavage confers neuroprotection with regard to prion diseases.
source: While α-cleavage, occurring in the middle of the PrPC sequence and producing a soluble N1 and a membrane-attached C1 fragment, confers neuroprotection with regard to prion diseases (Lewis et al., 2009; Westergard et al., 2011; Turnbaugh et al., 2012; Campbell et al., 2013) and Aβ-associated neurotoxicity (Guillot-Sestier et al., 2009; Resenberger et al., 2011; Beland et al., 2012; Guillot-Sestier et al., 2012; Fluharty et al., 2013), the role of an extreme C-terminal cleavage in close proximity to the plasma membrane, termed shedding, remains enigmatic.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior studies.

claim: α-cleavage confers neuroprotection with regard to Aβ-associated neurotoxicity.
source: While α-cleavage, occurring in the middle of the PrPC sequence and producing a soluble N1 and a membrane-attached C1 fragment, confers neuroprotection with regard to prion diseases (Lewis et al., 2009; Westergard et al., 2011; Turnbaugh et al., 2012; Campbell et al., 2013) and Aβ-associated neurotoxicity (Guillot-Sestier et al., 2009; Resenberger et al., 2011; Beland et al., 2012; Guillot-Sestier et al., 2012; Fluharty et al., 2013), the role of an extreme C-terminal cleavage in close proximity to the plasma membrane, termed shedding, remains enigmatic.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior studies.

claim: Shedding could be protective by reducing the substrate for prion conversion and the receptor for neurotoxicity.
source: On the one hand, by reducing the substrate for prion conversion and the receptor for neurotoxicity, this proteolytic release of almost full length PrPC from the plasma membrane could be protective with regard to prion diseases (Marella et al., 2002; Heiseke et al., 2008; Altmeppen et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Recombinant or transgenically expressed anchorless PrPC antagonizes PrPSc propagation.
source: Moreover, recombinant or transgenically expressed anchorless PrPC mimicking shed PrPC has been shown to antagonize both PrPSc propagation and Aβ neurotoxicity, respectively, thus indicating a protective activity by blocking toxic conformers and preventing their access to the cell (Meier et al., 2003; Calella et al., 2010; Nieznanski et al., 2012; Fluharty et al., 2013; Yuan et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior studies.

claim: Shedding could accelerate prion disease by increasing production and spread of anchorless prions within the CNS.
source: On the other hand, shedding could accelerate an ongoing prion disease by increasing production and subsequent spread of anchorless prions within the CNS.
evidence: This is a hypothesis presented by the authors.

claim: PrPSc can be shed from the cellular surface in vitro.
source: In fact, PrPSc can be shed from the cellular surface in vitro (Taylor et al., 2009) and anchorless PrPC can, in principle, be converted to PrPSc, resulting in an altered type of prion disease in transgenic mice (Chesebro et al., 2005, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Taylor et al., 2009.

claim: Anchorless PrPC can be converted to PrPSc.
source: In fact, PrPSc can be shed from the cellular surface in vitro (Taylor et al., 2009) and anchorless PrPC can, in principle, be converted to PrPSc, resulting in an altered type of prion disease in transgenic mice (Chesebro et al., 2005, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chesebro et al., 2005, 2010.

claim: High expression of anchorless PrPC leads to formation of prions and a late onset neurological disease.
source: High expression of anchorless PrPC leads to formation of prions and a late onset neurological disease (Stöhr et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Stöhr et al., 2011.

claim: ADAM10 is the relevant sheddase of PrPC in vivo.
source: While the in vivo identity of the protease(s) responsible for the α-cleavage of PrPC remains a matter of controversy (Vincent et al., 2001; Tveit et al., 2005; Taylor et al., 2009; Oliveira-Martins et al., 2010; Altmeppen et al., 2011, 2012; Beland et al., 2012; Liang et al., 2012; Wik et al., 2012; Mays et al., 2014; McDonald et al., 2014), we recently showed that a disintegrin and metalloproteinase ADAM10 is the relevant sheddase of PrPC in vivo (Altmeppen et al., 2011), as previously suggested (Parkin et al., 2004; Taylor et al., 2009) and subsequently confirmed (Wik et al., 2012; Ostapchenko et al., 2013; McDonald et al., 2014) by in vitro experiments of others.
evidence: This is supported by the authors' prior work and multiple citations.

claim: Depletion of ADAM10 in neural precursors abolishes shedding and leads to posttranslational accumulation of PrPC in the early secretory pathway.
source: Using conditional NestinADAM10 knockout mice (Jorissen et al., 2010), we recently showed that depletion of the protease in neural precursors abolishes shedding and leads to posttranslational accumulation of PrPC in the early secretory pathway indicative of a regulatory role of ADAM10 in PrPC membrane homeostasis (Altmeppen et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by the authors' prior work cited as Altmeppen et al., 2011.

claim: Membrane levels of PrPC were increased 1.56-fold in the absence of ADAM10 in neuronally differentiated NSCs.
source: As shown in Figure 1A, surface biotinylation experiments on neuronally differentiated NSCs revealed that membrane levels of PrPC were increased 1.56-fold (±0.12; SEM) in the absence of ADAM10 (n = 9 independent samples) compared with wild-type controls (set to 1 ± 0.13; n = 9).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Genetic reintroduction of Adam10 into NSC cultures of NestinA10 KO mice was sufficient to reduce membrane levels of PrPC.
source: Moreover, genetic reintroduction of Adam10 into NSC cultures of NestinA10 KO mice was sufficient to reduce membrane levels of PrPC (0.95 ± 0.11; n = 8) and thus to restore physiological wild-type conditions.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Nucleofection of NestinA10 KO cells with a vector lacking the Adam10 cDNA did not affect PrPC membrane levels.
source: Nucleofection of NestinA10 KO cells with a vector lacking the Adam10 cDNA did not show any effect on PrPC membrane levels (1.55 ± 0.18; n = 5).
evidence: This is a control experiment shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Increased total PrPC levels were found in ADAM10 knockout MEFs.
source: As expected, we found increased total PrPC levels in ADAM10 knockout MEFs by (i) immunofluorescence analysis of permeabilized cells (Figure 1C, upper part) and (ii) Western blot assessment of MEF lysates (Figure 1D, left part).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 1C and 1D.

claim: Colocalization was observed between ADAM10 and PrPC at the plasma membrane in wild-type MEFs.
source: In non-permeabilized wild-type MEFs, colocalization could be observed between the protease ADAM10 and its substrate PrPC at the plasma membrane (Figure 1C, bottom row).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Shedding is impaired in ADAM10 knockout MEFs compared with wild-type MEFs.
source: Results obtained with concentrated media and with immunoprecipitation of shed PrPC from media showed that shedding is impaired in ADAM10 knockout MEFs compared with wild-type MEFs (Figure 1D, right part).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Shedding of PrPC was absent in NestinA10 KO neurons.
source: Confirming our previous study (Altmeppen et al., 2011), shedding of PrPC was absent in NestinA10 KO neurons while tga20 neurons showed increased levels of shed PrPC compared with wild-type controls.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 1E and confirmed by prior work.

claim: tga20 neurons showed increased levels of shed PrPC compared with wild-type controls.
source: Confirming our previous study (Altmeppen et al., 2011), shedding of PrPC was absent in NestinA10 KO neurons while tga20 neurons showed increased levels of shed PrPC compared with wild-type controls.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Reduction of ADAM10 expression was accompanied by increased PrPC amounts in cortical homogenates at postnatal day 19.
source: First, we analyzed PrPC levels in A10 cKO and littermate controls at postnatal day (P) 19. Reduction of ADAM10 expression was accompanied by increased PrPC amounts as revealed by Western blot analysis of cortical homogenates (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Differences in ADAM10 expression and PrPC levels between A10 cKO and littermate controls were not seen in the cerebellum.
source: In contrast to the cortex, differences in ADAM10 expression and PrPC levels between A10 cKO and littermate controls were not seen in the cerebellum, a brain region not affected by our knockout strategy (Casanova et al., 2001; Prox et al., 2013) (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2A and citations to prior work.

claim: Increased PrPC levels in A10 cKO mice did not result from transcriptional upregulation.
source: Increased PrPC levels in A10 cKO mice did not result from transcriptional upregulation as there were no significant differences in PrPC mRNA levels in the forebrain at P19 as assessed by quantitative RT-PCR (mean ± SD: controls: 5.96 ± 0.86; A10 cKO: 6.32 ± 1.04; p = 0.23; n = 5) (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Adult A10 cKO mice did not show differences regarding weight and body size compared to controls.
source: In contrast to newborn A10 cKO mice (Prox et al., 2013), adult A10 cKO mice did not show differences regarding weight and body size (Figure 2D and Video 1).
evidence: This is an observational finding supported by Figure 2D and Video 1.

claim: Adult A10 cKO mice showed increased levels of PrPC in the cortex and hippocampus compared with their littermate controls at 35 weeks of age.
source: Again, as shown at P19, adult A10 cKO mice also showed increased levels of PrPC in the cortex and hippocampus compared with their littermate controls, as assessed by immunohistochemistry at 35 weeks of age (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: A10 cKO mice are viable and show a temporally unrestricted posttranslational increase of PrPC in neurons.
source: Taking these observations together, A10 cKO mice are viable and show a temporally unrestricted posttranslational increase of PrPC in neurons.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on multiple experimental findings presented in Figure 2.

claim: A10 cKO mice developed prion disease more than 40 days earlier than controls.
source: Our intracerebrally inoculated A10 cKO mice developed prion disease >40 days earlier than controls, corresponding to a shortening of incubation times of ∼30%.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by survival data shown in Figure 4 and Table 1.

claim: Incubation times until onset of terminal prion disease were significantly reduced in A10 cKO mice (103 ± 7 dpi) compared with littermate controls (146 ± 2 dpi).
source: Interestingly, we found significantly reduced incubation times until onset of terminal prion disease in the A10 cKO mice (103 ± 7 days post inoculation (dpi); SD) compared with littermate controls (146 ± 2 dpi) (Figure 4 and Table 1).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by survival data shown in Figure 4 and Table 1.

claim: Disease duration was comparable between A10 cKO mice (35 ± 4 days) and controls (40 ± 2.4 days).
source: Clinical manifestations (starting with a neglect of nest formation and fur cleaning, followed by presentation of a stiff tail and gait abnormalities, and terminating with kyphosis, weight loss, and hypoactivity) and disease duration (35 ± 4 days for A10 cKO mice and 40 ± 2.4 days for controls) were comparable between A10 cKO and littermate control mice (Figure 4, Table 1, Video 1).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 4, Table 1, and Video 1.

claim: tga20 mice showed fastest disease development and had to be sacrificed between 59 and 65 dpi.
source: In line with other studies (Fischer et al., 1996; Sandberg et al., 2011), tga20 mice showed fastest disease development and had to be sacrificed between 59 and 65 dpi (Figure 3) whereas mock-infected A10 cKO and control mice were taken out of the experiment at 200 dpi without any signs of prion disease (Figure 4 and Table 1).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by survival data shown in Figure 4 and Table 1, and confirmed by citations to prior work.

claim: Mock-infected A10 cKO and control mice were taken out of the experiment at 200 dpi without any signs of prion disease.
source: In line with other studies (Fischer et al., 1996; Sandberg et al., 2011), tga20 mice showed fastest disease development and had to be sacrificed between 59 and 65 dpi (Figure 3) whereas mock-infected A10 cKO and control mice were taken out of the experiment at 200 dpi without any signs of prion disease (Figure 4 and Table 1).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 4 and Table 1.

claim: Comparable levels of PrPSc were found in frontal brain homogenates of terminally diseased A10 cKO and control mice.
source: In terminally diseased mice, comparable levels of PrPSc were found in frontal brain homogenates of both genotypes as assessed by Western blot analysis after digestion of samples with PK (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: No differences in the PrPSc glycopattern between terminally diseased A10 cKO and control mice were detected.
source: No differences in the PrPSc glycopattern (Figure 5B) or sizes of PrPSc core fragments (Figure 5A) between terminally diseased A10 cKO and control mice were detected, which argues against the generation of a modified prion strain.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5A and 5B.

claim: No differences in sizes of PrPSc core fragments between terminally diseased A10 cKO and control mice were detected.
source: No differences in the PrPSc glycopattern (Figure 5B) or sizes of PrPSc core fragments (Figure 5A) between terminally diseased A10 cKO and control mice were detected, which argues against the generation of a modified prion strain.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Prion infection caused spongiform lesions, massive astrocytosis, and microgliosis in both A10 cKO and control genotypes.
source: Prion infection caused spongiform lesions, massive astrocytosis, and microgliosis in both genotypes (Figure 5C on the left).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by histological data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Similar levels of PrPSc immunopositivity were found at terminal stage of prion disease in A10 cKO and control mice.
source: Similar levels of PrPSc immunopositivity were found at this terminal stage of prion disease (Figure 5C), thus confirming our biochemical data (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Prion-diseased A10 cKO mice presented with an extraordinarily high abundance of tubulovesicular structures (TVS).
source: Remarkably, prion-diseased A10 cKO mice presented with an extraordinarily high abundance of tubulovesicular structures (TVS) (Figure 5—figure supplement 2) (Jeffrey and Fraser, 2000; Liberski et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Relative levels of total PrP were highest in tga20 mice (5.0 ± 0.3), with increased levels in A10 cKO mice (2.8 ± 0.4) compared with controls (set to 1 ± 0.1).
source: Relative levels of total PrP were highest in tga20 mice (5.0 ± 0.3; SEM), with increased levels in A10 cKO mice (2.8 ± 0.4) compared with controls (set to 1 ± 0.1) (A10 cKO vs control: **p = 0.0022; tga20 vs control: ***p = 0.0005; A10 cKO vs tga20: **p = 0.0015) (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Relative levels of PrPSc were significantly elevated in A10 cKO mice (3.9 ± 0.8), with moderate levels in littermate controls (set to 1 ± 0.2) and reduced levels in tga20 mice (0.6 ± 0.3).
source: Surprisingly, relative levels of PrPSc were significantly elevated in A10 cKO mice (3.9 ± 0.8), with moderate levels in littermate controls (set to 1 ± 0.2) and reduced levels in tga20 mice (0.6 ± 0.3) (A10 cKO vs control: *p = 0.049; A10 cKO vs tga20: *p = 0.032).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: A10 cKO mice showed significantly increased PrPSc formation compared with littermate controls and tga20 mice.
source: In summary, A10 cKO mice showed significantly increased PrPSc formation compared with littermate controls and tga20 mice, which cannot solely be explained by increased neuronal PrPC levels.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on Western blot data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Neuropathological changes in the forebrain, including spongiosis, astrocytosis and microgliosis, were more prominent in A10 cKO mice at 95 dpi.
source: Neuropathological changes in the forebrain, including spongiosis, astrocytosis and microgliosis, were more prominent in A10 cKO mice (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by histological data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: A10 cKO mice showed prominent PrPSc deposits in cortical and hippocampal regions at 95 dpi while controls and tga20 mice showed only moderate levels.
source: Remarkably, severe differences could be observed for PrPSc immunopositivity, with A10 cKO mice showing prominent PrPSc deposits in cortical and hippocampal regions while controls and tga20 mice showed only moderate levels, thus confirming the biochemical data (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: No significant differences in the activation state of Fyn and Erk1/2 kinases were observed in forebrain homogenates between tga20, A10 cKO, and littermate control mice at 95 dpi.
source: However, we did not observe any significant differences in the activation state of these kinases in forebrain homogenates between tga20, A10 cKO, and littermate control mice at the chosen time point (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Significant upregulation of calpain expression was found in A10 cKO mice (1.78 ± 0.24) compared with littermate controls (set to 1 ± 0.07) and tga20 mice (0.93 ± 0.14).
source: Interestingly, we found significant upregulation of calpain expression in A10 cKO mice (1.78 ± 0.24; SEM) compared with littermate controls (set to 1 ± 0.07; *p = 0.034) and tga20 mice (0.93 ± 0.14; *p = 0.022) (Figure 6D), thus correlating with PrPSc levels (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Calpain upregulation seemed to be specific for prion disease as no differences were detected in non-prion infected A10 cKO mice compared with age-matched wild-type controls.
source: This seemed to be specific for prion disease as no differences were detected in non-prion infected A10 cKO mice (mean: 0.90 ± 0.26 SEM; n = 4) when compared with age-matched wild-type controls (set to 1 ± 0.19; n = 5; p = 0.7) (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Prion titers increased with progression of disease and reached a plateau phase towards the terminal stage of disease.
source: Titers of infectious prions increased with progression of disease, showed only some inter-individual variation, and reached a plateau phase towards the terminal stage of disease.
evidence: This is a summary of bioassay results shown in Figure 7.

claim: Prion titers were independent of ADAM10 expression.
source: However, they were independent of ADAM10 expression since we did not find differences between the two genotypes.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on bioassay data shown in Figure 7.

claim: At early time points (35 dpi) prion titers were low (mean: A10 cKO: 3.9 ± 0.2 logLD50; control: 4.0 ± 0.2).
source: At early time points (35 dpi) prion titers were low (mean: A10 cKO: 3.9 ± 0.2 logLD50; control: 4.0 ± 0.2), intermediate titers were seen at 60 dpi (A10 cKO: 5.0 ± 0.5; control: 4.9 ± 0.8), and highest titers were observed in terminally ill mice (A10 cKO: 5.8 ± 0.2; control: 6.0 ± 0.2) (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by bioassay data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Intermediate prion titers were seen at 60 dpi (A10 cKO: 5.0 ± 0.5; control: 4.9 ± 0.8).
source: At early time points (35 dpi) prion titers were low (mean: A10 cKO: 3.9 ± 0.2 logLD50; control: 4.0 ± 0.2), intermediate titers were seen at 60 dpi (A10 cKO: 5.0 ± 0.5; control: 4.9 ± 0.8), and highest titers were observed in terminally ill mice (A10 cKO: 5.8 ± 0.2; control: 6.0 ± 0.2) (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by bioassay data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Highest prion titers were observed in terminally ill mice (A10 cKO: 5.8 ± 0.2; control: 6.0 ± 0.2).
source: At early time points (35 dpi) prion titers were low (mean: A10 cKO: 3.9 ± 0.2 logLD50; control: 4.0 ± 0.2), intermediate titers were seen at 60 dpi (A10 cKO: 5.0 ± 0.5; control: 4.9 ± 0.8), and highest titers were observed in terminally ill mice (A10 cKO: 5.8 ± 0.2; control: 6.0 ± 0.2) (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by bioassay data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Significantly increased PrPSc amounts in A10 cKO mice at 95 dpi did not result in elevated prion infectivity titers (A10 cKO: 5.74 ± 0.05; control: 5.66 ± 0.08; p = 0.2).
source: Interestingly, significantly increased PrPSc amounts in A10 cKO mice at 95 dpi (Figure 6A,B) did not result in elevated prion infectivity titers (A10 cKO: 5.74 ± 0.05; control: 5.66 ± 0.08; p = 0.2).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by bioassay data shown in Figure 7.

claim: An apparently reduced degree of spongiosis was found in the cerebellum and brain stem of A10 cKO mice compared with terminally diseased littermate controls.
source: Whereas for striatum we observed neuropathological changes typically found in terminal prion disease irrespective of the ADAM10 status, we found an apparently reduced degree of spongiosis in the cerebellum and brain stem of A10 cKO mice compared with terminally diseased littermate controls (Figure 8A and Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by histological data shown in Figure 8A and Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: PrPSc immunopositivity, astrocytosis involving Bergmann glia, and microglia activation were observed in the cerebellum of controls, but were virtually lacking in this brain region in A10 cKO mice at terminal disease.
source: In line with this, other prion-associated pathological hallmarks, including PrPSc immunopositivity, astrocytosis involving Bergmann glia, and microglia activation, were observed in the cerebellum of controls, but were virtually lacking in this brain region in A10 cKO mice (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: In the cerebellum and brain stem, relevant prion-typical neuropathological changes were observed in tga20 mice at 65 dpi but were almost absent in both A10 cKO and littermate controls at 95 dpi.
source: Interestingly, in the cerebellum and brain stem, relevant prion-typical neuropathological changes were observed in tga20 mice at 65 dpi but were almost absent in both A10 cKO and littermate controls at 95 dpi (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: The spatiotemporal data may indicate a correlation between PrPC shedding and the efficiency of prion spread within the brain.
source: Since tga20 mice show enhanced rates of PrPC shedding (Figure 1E) (Altmeppen et al., 2011), our spatiotemporal data may indicate a correlation between PrPC shedding and the efficiency of prion spread within the brain, with tga20 mice having the highest efficiency whereas A10 cKO mice show the least efficient dissemination of prion pathology (see model in Figure 9).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings, supported by data shown in Figures 1E, 8, and 9.

claim: α-cleavage-resistant PrPC deletion mutants are intrinsically neurotoxic upon expression in mice.
source: The protective role of α-cleavage is also supported by the fact that α-cleavage-resistant PrPC deletion mutants are intrinsically neurotoxic upon expression in mice (Shmerling et al., 1998; Baumann et al., 2007) (reviewed in Yusa et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: ADAM10 represents the principal PrPC sheddase in vivo.
source: In a previous study we have shown that ADAM10 represents the principal PrPC sheddase in vivo with lack of ADAM10 resulting in a posttranslational increase of PrPC levels (Altmeppen et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by the authors' prior work cited as Altmeppen et al., 2011.

claim: Lack of ADAM10 results in a posttranslational increase of PrPC levels.
source: In a previous study we have shown that ADAM10 represents the principal PrPC sheddase in vivo with lack of ADAM10 resulting in a posttranslational increase of PrPC levels (Altmeppen et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by the authors' prior work cited as Altmeppen et al., 2011.

claim: Prion-inoculated A10 cKO mice show considerably reduced incubation times.
source: In the present study we demonstrate that prion-inoculated A10 cKO mice show considerably reduced incubation times and increased conversion of PrPC to PrPSc.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by data shown in Figure 4 and Table 1.

claim: Prion-inoculated A10 cKO mice show increased conversion of PrPC to PrPSc.
source: In the present study we demonstrate that prion-inoculated A10 cKO mice show considerably reduced incubation times and increased conversion of PrPC to PrPSc.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Spread of prion pathology within the brain is reduced in A10 cKO mice.
source: In contrast, spread of prion pathology within the brain is reduced, thus indicating a dual role for ADAM10 in the pathophysiology of prion disease (Figure 9).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by data shown in Figure 8.

claim: ADAM10 acts as a sheddase for a number of neuronally expressed proteins with important functions in the development and homeostasis of the brain.
source: ADAM10 acts as a sheddase for a number of neuronally expressed proteins with important functions in the development and homeostasis of the brain (Yang et al., 2006; Weber and Saftig, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: It is now widely accepted that ADAM10 is the PrPC sheddase.
source: For PrPC it is now widely accepted that ADAM10 is the PrPC sheddase (Parkin et al., 2004; Taylor et al., 2009; Altmeppen et al., 2011; Wik et al., 2012; Ostapchenko et al., 2013; McDonald et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Lack of ADAM10 results in elevated membrane levels of PrPC.
source: In addition to accumulation of PrPC in the early secretory pathway (Altmeppen et al., 2011), we here show that lack of ADAM10 also results in elevated membrane levels of PrPC.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by data shown in Figure 1.

claim: ADAM10-mediated shedding controls PrPC membrane homeostasis.
source: This supports a model where ADAM10-mediated shedding controls PrPC membrane homeostasis (Altmeppen et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a model proposed by the authors based on their findings and supported by citation to their prior work.

claim: Incubation time after intracerebral inoculation is mainly influenced by PrPC levels.
source: In contrast to peripheral prion inoculation where the integrity of the lymphoreticular or autonomous nervous system plays a decisive role in neuroinvasion of prions, incubation time after intracerebral inoculation is mainly influenced by PrPC levels (Mabbott et al., 2000; Glatzel et al., 2001; Prinz et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Dramatic reductions in incubation times upon intracerebral inoculation with high-dose RML prions have so far only been achieved when PrPC is massively overexpressed.
source: Such dramatic reductions upon intracerebral inoculation with high-dose RML prions have so far only been achieved when PrPC is massively overexpressed (Fischer et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Fischer et al., 1996.

claim: Transgenic overexpression of bovine ADAM10 in mice led to prolongation of prion disease.
source: The only other study investigating the role of ADAM10 in prion disease showed that transgenic overexpression of bovine ADAM10 in mice led to prolongation of prion disease (Endres et al., 2009), a finding which is complementary to our data on the effect of ADAM10 deficiency.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Endres et al., 2009.

claim: Transcriptional regulation of PrPC is not affected by ADAM10.
source: In contrast, data from the present and previous studies show that transcriptional regulation of PrPC is not affected by ADAM10 whereas proteolytic processing clearly is (Parkin et al., 2004; Taylor et al., 2009; Altmeppen et al., 2011; Wik et al., 2012; Ostapchenko et al., 2013; McDonald et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by data from the present study (Figure 2C) and multiple citations to prior work.

claim: A10 cKO mice show learning deficits.
source: Indeed, ADAM10 is involved in a number of developmental and immunological processes and A10 cKO mice show learning deficits (Weber and Saftig, 2012; Prox et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: A10 cKO mice do not show any gross morphological abnormalities in the CNS.
source: Furthermore, A10 cKO mice do not show any gross morphological abnormalities in the CNS, have a normal life span once they have survived a critical weaning period, and mock inoculated mice behave normally (Prox et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Prox et al., 2013.

claim: A10 cKO mice have a normal life span once they have survived a critical weaning period.
source: Furthermore, A10 cKO mice do not show any gross morphological abnormalities in the CNS, have a normal life span once they have survived a critical weaning period, and mock inoculated mice behave normally (Prox et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Prox et al., 2013.

claim: Mock inoculated A10 cKO mice behave normally.
source: Furthermore, A10 cKO mice do not show any gross morphological abnormalities in the CNS, have a normal life span once they have survived a critical weaning period, and mock inoculated mice behave normally (Prox et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Prox et al., 2013 and data from the present study.

claim: Increased PrPSc levels found in A10 cKO mice strongly argue in favor of PrP-dependent effects of ADAM10 depletion.
source: Finally, we consider that increased PrPSc levels found in A10 cKO mice strongly argue in favor of PrP-dependent effects of ADAM10 depletion.
evidence: This is an interpretation by the authors based on their experimental findings.

claim: Tga20 mice are hypersensitive to prion disease yet do not show significant levels of PrPSc even though PrPC is strongly overexpressed.
source: Tga20 mice are hypersensitive to prion disease yet do not show significant levels of PrPSc even though PrPC is strongly overexpressed.
evidence: This is an observation from the study, supported by data shown in Figure 6.

claim: ADAM10-mediated shedding of PrPC in neurons of tga20 mice is increased approximately threefold.
source: In a previous study we have shown and re-evaluated here that ADAM10-mediated shedding of PrPC in neurons of tga20 mice is increased approximately threefold (Altmeppen et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by the authors' prior work and data from the present study shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Soluble GPI-anchorless forms of PrPC impair PrPSc formation.
source: Of note, soluble GPI-anchorless forms of PrPC, which may be regarded as correlates of shed PrPC, and experimentally-induced release of PrPC in vitro impair PrPSc formation (Marella et al., 2002; Meier et al., 2003; Kim et al., 2009; Yuan et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior studies.

claim: High levels of shed PrPC in tga20 mice may impair PrPSc formation.
source: Thus, high levels of shed PrPC in tga20 mice may impair PrPSc formation whereas lack of shed PrPC in A10 cKO mice may favor PrPSc formation (Figure 9).
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their findings and prior literature.

claim: Lack of shed PrPC in A10 cKO mice may favor PrPSc formation.
source: Thus, high levels of shed PrPC in tga20 mice may impair PrPSc formation whereas lack of shed PrPC in A10 cKO mice may favor PrPSc formation (Figure 9).
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their findings.

claim: PrPSc production was decreased in mice moderately overexpressing ADAM10.
source: In line with this concept, PrPSc production was decreased in mice moderately overexpressing ADAM10 (Endres et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Endres et al., 2009.

claim: Increased levels of PrPC at the plasma membrane should facilitate PrPC-mediated neurotoxicity and thereby determine incubation times in both tga20 and A10 cKO mice.
source: In both tga20 and A10 cKO mice, increased levels of PrPC at the plasma membrane should facilitate PrPC-mediated neurotoxicity and thereby determine incubation times.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their findings.

claim: The data provide a potential explanation for the tga20 paradox of low PrPSc formation despite high PrPC levels and short incubation times.
source: Interestingly, these data provide a potential explanation for the tga20 paradox of low PrPSc formation despite high PrPC levels and short incubation times (Fischer et al., 1996).
evidence: This is an interpretation by the authors based on their findings.

claim: A10 cKO mice and controls showed identical prion titers.
source: A10 cKO mice and controls showed identical prion titers.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by bioassay data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Titers of prion infectivity, PrPSc, and the presence of potentially neurotoxic PrP conformers are not congruent.
source: It is becoming increasingly evident that titers of prion infectivity, PrPSc, and the presence of potentially neurotoxic PrP conformers are not congruent (Lasmezas et al., 1997; Barron et al., 2007; Piccardo et al., 2007; Krasemann et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior studies.

claim: ADAM10-mediated shedding affects formation of PrPSc while it does not influence production of 'prions'.
source: In fact, the exact composition of infectious 'prions' (i.e., the entity determined by bioassay) is not fully understood and it may be that ADAM10-mediated shedding affects formation of PrPSc while it does not influence production of 'prions'.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors to explain their findings.

claim: Prion-infected mice expressing anchorless PrPC show PrPSc formation and deposition in ectopic sites.
source: In view of the fact that prion-infected mice expressing anchorless PrPC show PrPSc formation and deposition in ectopic sites (Lee et al., 2011) and prion propagation in the CNS (Chesebro et al., 2005), we investigated whether shedding contributes to the spread of prion pathology.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Prion-infected mice expressing anchorless PrPC show prion propagation in the CNS.
source: In view of the fact that prion-infected mice expressing anchorless PrPC show PrPSc formation and deposition in ectopic sites (Lee et al., 2011) and prion propagation in the CNS (Chesebro et al., 2005), we investigated whether shedding contributes to the spread of prion pathology.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chesebro et al., 2005.

claim: A10 cKO mice show prion-related pathology and PrPSc deposition at the site of and adjacent to prion administration, whereas brain regions distant from the inoculation site were unaffected, even at terminal stages of disease.
source: In fact, A10 cKO mice show prion-related pathology and PrPSc deposition at the site of (striatum) and adjacent to prion administration (hippocampus, frontal cortex, thalamus), whereas brain regions distant from the inoculation site (cerebellum, brain stem) were unaffected, even at terminal stages of disease.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by data shown in Figure 8.

claim: In tga20 mice, dissemination of prion-related pathology occurred efficiently at a much earlier time point.
source: In contrast, in tga20 mice, dissemination of prion-related pathology occurred efficiently at a much earlier time point.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by data shown in Figure 8.

claim: The influence of the immune system, including microglial activation on intracerebral spread of prions, is limited.
source: However, the influence of the immune system, including microglial activation on intracerebral spread of prions, is limited, therefore a correlation between PrP shedding and the efficiency of prion spread is possible (Glatzel et al., 2004; Grizenkova et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Upon prion infection of mice, heterozygous expression of normal and anchorless PrP results in earlier death compared with wild-type mice.
source: In line with our findings, it has been shown that, upon prion infection of mice, heterozygous expression of normal and anchorless PrP results in earlier death compared with wild-type mice (Chesebro et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chesebro et al., 2005.

claim: Shedding of either PrPC or PrPSc should be considered as an alternative mechanism of prion spread.
source: Thus, shedding of either PrPC (followed by cell-free conversion [Kocisko et al., 1994]) or PrPSc, both of which have been shown to occur (Taylor et al., 2009; Altmeppen et al., 2011), should be considered as an alternative mechanism of prion spread (Figure 9) aside from direct transsynaptic cell-to-cell transfer (Glatzel et al., 2001; Shearin and Bessen, 2014), exosomal (Alais et al., 2008) and viral transfer (Leblanc et al., 2006), or tunneling nanotubes (Gousset et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their findings and supported by multiple citations.

claim: Proteolytic processing represents a master switch in the pathophysiology of prion diseases by drastically affecting PrPSc formation and incubation times.
source: In conclusion, our data indicate that proteolytic processing, as described here for the shedding of the prion protein, represents a master switch in the pathophysiology of prion diseases by drastically affecting PrPSc formation and incubation times.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, based on multiple experimental findings.

claim: A reduction of ADAM10 in prion disease has recently been reported in vitro and in vivo.
source: Interestingly, protective effects of ADAM10 might be hijacked in prion diseases since a reduction of the protease in prion disease has recently been reported in vitro and in vivo (Chen et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chen et al., 2014.

claim: In other neurodegenerative proteinopathies where PrPC-PrPSc conversion does not play a role, ADAM10-mediated shedding of PrPC might solely be protective.
source: Apart from prion disease, in other neurodegenerative proteinopathies, where PrPC-PrPSc conversion does not play a role, ADAM10-mediated shedding of PrPC might solely be protective due to reduction of the receptor as well as the production of a soluble blocker of toxic oligomers.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their findings.
